name: Jira Cloud (OAuth 2.0 3LO)
summary: Create an OAuth 2.0 (3LO) integration in the Atlassian developer console, add Jira scopes and a callback, run the authorization code flow, then find the user's site (cloudid) before calling the Jira API. Our hands-on check stopped at the developer-terms checkbox, so later steps are documentation-backed only.

active.basis: No end-to-end run was completed, so no effort figure is claimed.

wait.basis: Sharing is a console toggle per the docs; no page we checked states a review wait. Marketplace listing is separate and was not researched.

prerequisites.text: An Atlassian account that can open the developer console.

source.quote: OAuth 2.0 (3LO) apps are created and managed in the developer console.

prerequisites.text: A Jira Cloud user with the Jira permissions your operations need; scopes never exceed the user's own permissions.

source.quote: Note, the permissions held by the user an app is acting for always constrain the app, regardless of the app's scopes.

steps.title: Use OAuth 2.0 (3LO), not API tokens
steps.detail: Atlassian recommends 3LO for integrations that are not Connect or Forge apps.

source.quote: OAuth 2.0 authorization code grants (3LO) : This is the recommended method.

steps.title: Plan one distributable app for all customers
steps.detail: Do not ask each customer to create their own 3LO app or hand you API tokens; Atlassian says that breaks its security requirements.

source.quote: Build a single, distributable 3LO app for your integration.

steps.title: Create the OAuth 2.0 integration
steps.detail: Developer console → Create → OAuth 2.0 integration, then enter a name. On 2026-10-28 we reached this form; creation requires accepting Atlassian's developer terms, which only the account owner should do, so we stopped there.

source.quote: In the Developer console, select the Create dropdown and choose OAuth 2.0 integration to create an OAuth 2.0 (3LO) app.

steps.title: Choose account-level or resource-level grant

settings.value: Consent covers the user's Atlassian account
settings.explain: Pick when one consent should reach every site the user can access.
Pick when users should choose exactly which sites the app may touch. We selected this in our draft form.

steps.detail: Both options were shown in the create form we observed. Whether the choice can be changed later was not established.

source.quote: Resource-level grant: The user’s consent is limited to the specific site(s) they select on the consent screen.

steps.title: Add the Jira API and only the scopes your operations need
steps.detail: Under Permissions, add the Jira API and configure scopes. Read each endpoint's "OAuth scopes required" field; prefer classic scopes. Changing scopes later makes existing users consent again.

source.quote: Consult the Jira Cloud platform REST API documentation to determine the scope needed for each operation and create a list of scopes.

steps.title: Configure the callback URL
steps.detail: Authorization → Configure next to OAuth 2.0 (3LO) → Callback URL. Use your agent application's backend callback (e.g. https://your-agent.example/auth/jira/callback, illustrative). Whether localhost is accepted was not established.

source.quote: When you implement OAuth 2.0 (3LO) in your app (see next section), the redirect_uri must match this URL.

steps.title: Copy Client ID and Secret into your backend secret store
steps.detail: Both are under Settings for the app. The secret is needed for the code exchange; keep it server-side only.

source.quote: client_secret : ( required ) Set this to the Secret for your app.

steps.title: Send the user to the authorization URL with a user-bound state
steps.detail: https://auth.atlassian.com/authorize with audience=api.atlassian.com, client_id, scope, redirect_uri, state, response_type=code and prompt=consent. Check state on return.

source.quote: Set this to a value that is associated with the user you are directing to the authorization URL

steps.title: Exchange the code for an access token
steps.detail: POST JSON to https://auth.atlassian.com/oauth/token with grant_type=authorization_code, client_id, client_secret, code and the same redirect_uri.

source.quote: If successful, the user will be redirected to the app's callback URL, with an authorization code provided as a query parameter called code.

steps.title: Find the user's site (cloudid)
steps.detail: The token works across sites, so pick the intended site's id from this list.

source.quote: Make a GET request to https://api.atlassian.com/oauth/token/accessible-resources passing the access token as a bearer token in the header of the request.

steps.title: Call Jira through the API gateway
steps.detail: Requests go to api.atlassian.com, not your-site.atlassian.net, with Authorization: Bearer <token>.

steps.title: Request offline_access if you need long-lived access
steps.detail: Refresh tokens rotate: store the new one each time you use it.

source.quote: To get a refresh token in your initial authorization flow, add offline_access to the scope parameter of the authorization URL.

steps.title: Enable sharing before other users can connect
steps.detail: Distribution → Enable sharing. This is not a Marketplace listing.

source.quote: If you want to distribute your app to other users, you must enable sharing.

gaps.text: No app has been created yet: creation needs the account owner to accept Atlassian's developer terms. Callback, scopes, credentials, consent and API calls are unobserved.
gaps.next_action: Account owner reviews and accepts the terms, then we rerun the hands-on check.
